title: After a Week of Outages, More Americans Are Stocking Up — Just in Case
summary:
Teri Brown has been worried about what her family would do if the U.S. electrical grid went down. She is also concerned about artificial intelligence and political unrest. So she and her husband Richard got to work, stocking their home in the Denver suburbs with food, some of which they have started freeze drying, and two 55-gallon tanks to hold extra water.

They are now what many people would call 'preppers' — people who get ready for worst-case scenarios. Brown, 47, says the label comes with a stigma. In popular culture, preppers are often portrayed as extremists stockpiling food in the woods to get ready for the apocalypse.

That image might be changing, thanks to a series of tech outages. In the last week, Microsoft suffered an outage that kept Outlook users from their email. Then users could not access Apple Pay. Most disruptive was last Friday's nationwide ground stop at airports.

The outages have left many feeling unprepared, and many are now turning to preppers for survival tips. Krystal Christensen, who posts videos to more than 400,000 followers and subscribers, says she is seeing ten times as many people asking questions. She tells viewers to buy only what their household needs and eats, and she strongly discourages panic buying.

It has been happening anyway. Christensen posted a video from her Costco in Utah showing generators down to a few boxes, and longtime prepper Derrick James said an emergency radio he mentioned sold out in two days on Amazon.

Deanne Criswell, the former head of the Federal Emergency Management Agency under President Biden, says people should prepare for the risks where they live, not panic-buy. Monique Imroth, 64, of San Diego County, agrees — her risk is wildfires. 'You're prepping for whatever weird thing happens on Tuesday,' she said.
why_it_matters: Outages can suddenly cut off email, payments and travel, so knowing how to prepare calmly for the risks where you live matters for every family.

keywords.explanation: The grid is the network of wires and power stations that carries electricity to homes and businesses.
A stigma is a feeling of shame or disapproval that people attach to a person or a label.
The apocalypse is an imagined event in which the world as we know it comes to an end.
A ground stop is an order that keeps planes on the ground and stops them from taking off.
Panic buying is buying a lot of something all at once because people are afraid it will run out.

background_read: Preppers are people who stock up on food, water and supplies so their families can cope if something goes wrong, such as a power cut or a storm.
The electrical grid is the network that carries electricity to homes, and many everyday services such as email, payments and flights depend on it working.
When a service stops working for many people at once, that is called an outage, and it can leave people feeling unprepared.
Emergency experts say the best way to prepare is to plan for the risks that are most likely where you live, rather than buying far more than you need.
